title: Early HT capacity adaptation when groups slightly exceed initial sink capacity
hypothesis: With >2 threads, RadixHTConfig::SinkCapacity() gives each thread a 32768-slot aggregate HT, so it resizes at ResizeThreshold = 21845 entries. DecideAdaptation(), the only thing that can grow the HT, runs only once a thread has sunk ADAPTIVITY_THRESHOLD = 1,048,576 rows. q16 puts ~1.18M rows into 27,839 groups (above 21845). In the distinct-finalize phase (HashAggregateDistinctFinalizeTask::AggregateDistinctGrouping, which sinks into grouping_data.table_data.Sink), each of the 8 tasks gets ~150k rows covering nearly all groups. No thread reaches 1M rows, so the HT never grows. It fills and is Abandon()ed about 7 times per thread, materialising many copies of each group, and RadixPartitionedHashTable finalize then has to combine several hundred thousand rows instead of ~27k per thread. Measured: the same join with a plain GROUP BY brand,type,size count() takes 178 ms, against 121 ms without the GROUP BY. That is ~60 ms for 1.18M rows into 27k groups, ~400 ns/row of CPU, which is pathological. count(DISTINCT) adds ~45 ms more through the same path.
plan: In src/execution/radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp, RadixPartitionedHashTable::Sink: just after the `if (ht.Count() + STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE < ResizeThreshold(local_sink_capacity)) return;` early-out (the HT is full) and before the Abandon() call, add an early check that can only grow the HT. Conditions: !lstate.adapted && gstate.number_of_threads > GROW_STRATEGY_THREAD_THRESHOLD (so HLL is enabled) && !gstate.external && lstate.local_sink_capacity < ADAPTIVITY_THRESHOLD && ht.GetSinkCount() >= 2 * ResizeThreshold(local_sink_capacity), so there are enough samples. Compute deduplicated_count = ht.GetMaterializedCount(), hll_count = MinValue(ht.GetHLLUpperBound(), deduplicated_count) and the same percentages as DecideAdaptation. If deduplicated_pct / hll_pct > 2.0 (CAPACITY_INCREASE_DEDUPLICATION_RATE_THRESHOLD), set new_capacity = MinValue(GetCapacityForCount(hll_count), ADAPTIVITY_THRESHOLD). If new_capacity > local_sink_capacity, set lstate.local_sink_capacity = new_capacity, call ht.Abandon(); ht.Resize(new_capacity); and return. Do not set adapted, so the existing 1M-row DecideAdaptation still runs later, and do NOT take the SkipLookups branch early. Best done as a small helper next to DecideAdaptation, perhaps sharing the math. Memory per thread stays bounded by the existing ADAPTIVITY_THRESHOLD cap. Also check the MaybeRepartition path that follows, which must still run when no resize happens.
expected_gain: q16: 10-20% (the main-HT sink and finalize in count(DISTINCT) finalize, ~27k groups). Any hash GROUP BY with roughly 22k-700k groups and fewer than 1M rows per thread gains similarly.
generality: Any parallel hash aggregation whose group count exceeds the initial 32k-slot capacity but whose per-thread input is below 1M rows. That is common for medium-cardinality GROUP BYs on joins or filtered scans, and in the count(DISTINCT) finalize phase. Possible slowdowns: inputs where the HLL early sample overestimates the dedup benefit (cost: a larger HT, at most the existing cap), and a slightly larger per-thread HT that falls out of L2.
risk: Low. The change can only grow capacity, within existing caps, using the same mechanism DecideAdaptation already uses (Abandon + Resize), so correctness is unaffected. External/out-of-core mode is excluded. The 2-thread grow strategy is untouched.

title: Perfect hash join for sparse-but-bounded key ranges
hypothesis: q16's inner join on ps_partkey = p_partkey has a 296k-row build side with key range ~2M. PerfectHashJoinExecutor::CanDoPerfectHashJoin rejects it because MAX_BUILD_SIZE = 1048576 (absolute range cap). The probe takes 0.25 s cumulative for 1.24M probe rows (~200 ns/row per thread) and is the largest operator after the aggregate. A perfect HJ replaces hash, pointer chase and key compare with a direct index.
plan: In src/execution/operator/join/perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp CanDoPerfectHashJoin, allow build_range up to a larger cap (e.g. 4M) when the density ht.Count()/build_range is at least ~1/8, keeping the existing 1M absolute cap otherwise. Check the memory estimate (build_size * sum of rhs column widths) against the temporary memory or available memory. FullScanHashTable is single-threaded, so measure the build cost.
expected_gain: q16 ~5-10% if the probe gets 2x faster.
generality: Joins on integer surrogate keys whose build side is filtered (a dense domain with a selective filter on the dimension). Possible slowdowns: memory overhead and the single-threaded build for wide build payloads.
risk: Medium. Memory amplification (range * row width) and the single-threaded build could hurt larger builds. Needs a memory guard.

title: Enforce pushed IN-list filter in scan instead of mark join
hypothesis: The part scan emits 1.86M rows that the `optional: p_size IN (...)` filter does not reduce. InClauseRewriter (src/optimizer/in_clause_rewriter.cpp) turns IN lists with >=6 constants into a MARK join + FILTER, and the scan applies only an optional zonemap filter. A scan-level IN filter would cut the scan output to 296k and remove the mark join.
plan: Investigate why the pushed IN filter is optional (filter pushdown of IN to TableFilter) and whether constant IN lists of moderate size (< some N) on scan columns could stay as an IN expression filter evaluated in the scan instead of the mark join rewrite.
expected_gain: q16 small (~2-4%): build-side pipeline ~0.13 s cumulative.
generality: Any scan with a constant IN list of 6+ values.
risk: Low-medium. Optimizer change; plan shapes change for many queries.

title: Cut per-row VARCHAR-key overhead in radix hash aggregate (sink/repartition/combine)
hypothesis: Measured with EXPLAIN ANALYZE at 8 threads. q16 as written: HASH_GROUP_BY 0.65-0.70s CPU, 255-309 ms total. The same query with the VARCHAR group key p_type replaced by hash(p_type) (BIGINT): HASH_GROUP_BY 0.23s, 169 ms total. With substr(p_type,1,12) (an inlined VARCHAR, 5x fewer groups) it is still 0.56s. A plain GROUP BY on brand,type,size,suppkey (1.18M groups, which is the distinct phase) costs 0.85s on its own. So the overhead is in the VARCHAR layout path itself (layout !AllConstant) and does not depend on heap pointer chasing or on group count. It is mostly in the high-cardinality first (distinct) phase. Candidates I found by reading the code: (a) with radix_bits >= UNPARTITIONED_RADIX_BITS_THRESHOLD (3), and the sink starts at that with 8 threads, every Abandon() (aggregate_hashtable.cpp:129-138) runs unpartitioned_data->Repartition into partitioned_data. That is a second full copy of every row. For heap layouts it also copies heap data and recomputes pointers, and a near-unique HT abandons every ~21.8k rows. (b) PartitionedTupleData::Append (partitioned_tuple_data.cpp:55-88) runs ComputeHeapSizes plus a per-partition heap BuildBufferSpace on each chunk. (c) The finalize Combine (aggregate_hashtable.cpp:883) re-gathers and re-scatters all strings. Fixing whichever dominates should move VARCHAR-key aggregation toward the fixed-width cost.
plan: 1) Measure first, then fix. Add temporary timers (or rebuild variants) around these phases for the q16 shape (the variant with hash(p_type) is the fast reference): GroupedAggregateHashTable::FindOrCreateGroups / partitioned append, Abandon() -> unpartitioned_data->Repartition, the RadixHTLocalSourceState::Finalize -> ht->Combine path, and Scan. 2) Fix the dominant phase. Preferred if (a) dominates: for layouts that are not AllConstant, skip the unpartitioned staging and append directly into partitioned_data. Do this by not using the UNPARTITIONED_RADIX_BITS_THRESHOLD path when the layout has heap columns, gated in GroupedAggregateHashTable where unpartitioned_data is chosen (aggregate_hashtable.cpp ~line 60-140 and the FindOrCreateGroups append site). Alternatively make Repartition for heap layouts reuse the existing heap blocks. If (b) dominates: skip ComputeHeapSizes/heap buffer work for chunks whose VARCHAR values are all inlined. If (c) dominates: report the findings without forcing a fix. 3) Remove the timers and verify with dbe-tool bench.
expected_gain: q16 10-30%. The hash(p_type) experiment bounds the attainable gain at ~85 ms of ~255 ms if VARCHAR-key aggregation were as cheap as fixed-width.
generality: Any GROUP BY or count(DISTINCT) with string keys and medium-to-high group cardinality on multiple threads. This is very common (TPC-H q10/q13/q16/q18-style, string dimension keys). Possible slowdowns: skipping unpartitioned staging may cost cache misses when partitions are many and rows wide. Gate it on heap layouts only and check that low-cardinality string group-bys do not regress.
risk: Medium. Aggregate HT internals with heap-pointer invariants (pin states, heap pointer recompute) can cause subtle corruption. Correctness is checked on hidden queries, so keep the change minimal and run the aggregate tests. Risk of no clear fix if the cost is spread across phases. If so, report the per-phase breakdown.

title: Early tentative SkipLookups for near-unique radix aggregate sinks
hypothesis: In q16 the count(DISTINCT) aggregate first sinks into a distinct radix table keyed on (brand, type, size, suppkey). Those keys are almost all unique. A plain GROUP BY on the same 4 keys returns 1,184,608 groups from 1,184,892 input rows, and its HASH_GROUP_BY alone takes 0.84 s CPU, more than the 0.67 s the whole distinct aggregate takes. Each of the 8 threads sees only about 150k rows. That is far below ADAPTIVITY_THRESHOLD = 1M, so DecideAdaptation (radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp:424) never fires and the table never switches to SkipLookups, even though it has a hll_percentage > 0.95 rule written for exactly this case. So every row pays for the probe, key compare (on a VARCHAR key), HT insert and unpartitioned staging. Then about every 21845 rows the HT is Abandon()ed (32768 capacity), having deduplicated nothing. E0002 measured this sink at about 253 ms CPU for AddChunk, 40 ms for Abandon and 100-146 ms for MaybeRepartition/staging, about 400 ms of roughly 1.44 s total CPU. All of that dedup work is redone in the finalize Combine anyway. With SkipLookups the sink only hashes and appends straight to partitioned_data. That also bypasses the unpartitioned staging and repartition that E0002 found to be the VARCHAR-specific cost.
plan: In src/execution/radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp, RadixPartitionedHashTable::Sink, at the point where `ht.Abandon()` is called (more than 2 threads, not external), add an early, reversible adaptation while `!lstate.adapted`. Right after the Abandon, compute sink_count = ht.GetSinkCount(), hll = MinValue(ht.GetHLLUpperBound(), sink_count) and materialized = ht.GetMaterializedCount(). If hll/sink_count > 0.95 AND materialized/sink_count > 0.95, call ht.SkipLookups(). The second test is the HT's actual dedup, so data with real duplicates inside one HT fill never triggers. Otherwise, if lookups are currently skipped, turn them back on. Add `void GroupedAggregateHashTable::SetSkipLookups(bool)`, or `EnableLookups()`, in src/execution/aggregate_hashtable.cpp and src/include/duckdb/execution/aggregate_hashtable.hpp. Toggling right after Abandon is safe because the pointer table is cleared and count is 0. Keep the HLL enabled and leave `adapted` false, so the existing 1M-row DecideAdaptation still makes the final call. Optionally, when hll_pct exceeds 0.95 there, it keeps skip_lookups. When the data later turns duplicate-heavy, the re-check at the next abandon (each fill, about 21k rows) re-enables lookups. Do not touch the grow-strategy path (2 threads or fewer). Validate with q16, with a plain high-cardinality GROUP BY, and with a low-cardinality GROUP BY such as 25k groups over 10M rows, to confirm that one does not trigger. Using hash(p_type) in the query is a cheap way to bisect.
expected_gain: q16 8-15%. It should remove most of the roughly 300-400 ms CPU of probe, abandon and staging work in the distinct-table sink. The finalize Combine sees the same row count as before, because the HT deduplicated nothing.
generality: Any count(DISTINCT x) GROUP BY g, where (g, x) is near-unique, and any high-cardinality GROUP BY or DISTINCT with fewer than 1M rows per thread (about 8M total at 8 threads), the size where the existing adaptation never fires. Possible slowdowns: data whose first ~20k rows per thread are unique but which has many duplicates later. The per-fill HLL re-check bounds that to at most one fill of skipped dedup per transition.
risk: Low to medium. SkipLookups is an existing, correctness-safe mode: the finalize always deduplicates. The main risk is a performance regression on data that is unique early and duplicated later, which the reversible check mitigates. HLL accuracy at about 20k rows is a few percent, so the 0.95 threshold has some margin.

title: Cut non-inlined VARCHAR group-key overhead in the radix aggregate (measure per phase, fix the largest delta)
hypothesis: In the q16 count(DISTINCT) aggregate, a non-inlined VARCHAR group key (p_type, 25 chars, which CompressedMaterialization cannot pack because it is longer than 16 bytes) roughly doubles the aggregate's cost. Planner A/B on a temp table of the q16 join output (1.18M rows), 8 threads, warm: `SELECT hb, h, p_size, count(DISTINCT ps_suppkey) ... GROUP BY ALL` with h = hash(p_type) BIGINT gives HASH_GROUP_BY 0.10 s CPU and 45-48 ms wall. The same query with p_type VARCHAR gives 0.22 s CPU and 82-87 ms wall. The scan is 0.01 s in both, so the difference is inside the aggregate. Weaker evidence: SELECT DISTINCT on the 4 keys is 46-59 ms with p_type vs 35-37 ms with h, and a plain GROUP BY count(*) over 28k groups is 34-46 ms vs 20 ms. In q16 the aggregate is about 90 of the ~155 ms wall (the join-only query is 62 ms warm), so removing most of this ~100 ns/row string penalty is worth ~25-40 ms. Rows carrying a non-inlined string go through several stages: distinct-HT AppendUnified, which computes heap sizes and scatters into the heap; abandon/repartition, which copies the heap and recomputes pointers (TupleDataAllocator::RecomputeHeapPointers); the distinct finalize GroupedAggregateHashTable::Combine, which gathers via FlushMoveState and re-scatters new groups with another heap copy; then a re-hash and re-sink into the main HT, and the main finalize Combine. Earlier sink-side tweaks (E0001-E0003) never isolated the string cost.
plan: Step 1, measure (cheap). Add temporary timers following the E0002 pattern: Printer::RawPrint from gstate destructors. Time these phases: RadixPartitionedHashTable::Sink (FindOrCreateGroups / AppendUnified), MaybeRepartition, RadixHTLocalSourceState::Finalize -> GroupedAggregateHashTable::Combine (src/execution/aggregate_hashtable.cpp:883), the re-sink in HashAggregateDistinctFinalizeTask::AggregateDistinctGrouping (physical_hash_aggregate.cpp:648-754), and the main finalize. Run the temp-table A/B twice: `CREATE TEMP TABLE t AS SELECT p_brand, p_type, p_size, ps_suppkey, hash(p_type) h, hash(p_brand) hb FROM <q16 join>`, then compare GROUP BY hb,h,p_size against hb,p_type,p_size with count(DISTINCT ps_suppkey). Find the phase with the largest VARCHAR-vs-BIGINT delta. Inside it, look at per-chunk heap work in src/common/types/row/ (tuple_data_collection.cpp, tuple_data_allocator.cpp, tuple_data_scatter_gather.cpp): ComputeHeapSizes, Build, RecomputeHeapPointers or FindHeapPointers on scan or pin, and chunk-part splitting when 300-row input chunks each open new heap parts. Step 2: fix that one mechanism. Candidate fixes, depending on the evidence: (a) skip RecomputeHeapPointers or the heap-pointer search when the heap blocks have not moved (in-memory, still pinned); (b) in Combine and Repartition of heap layouts, copy row and heap data in bulk per chunk part instead of per row; (c) avoid creating many small heap chunk parts for small input chunks. Keep the diff to one mechanism.
expected_gain: q16 10-25%. The aggregate is ~90 of ~155 ms, and the string penalty measured on the same data is ~40 ms wall.
generality: Any hash aggregate, DISTINCT, or count(DISTINCT) grouped by strings longer than 12 bytes (names, types, comments, URLs). These are very common in analytical workloads. Joins and sorts also benefit if the fix lands in shared TupleData code. Risk of slowdown: little, if the change only removes redundant work. Spilling (external) aggregates must keep the pointer recomputation that unpin/repin needs.
risk: Medium. TupleData heap-pointer invariants are subtle; skipping a recompute when blocks did move corrupts strings. Must test the external/spill path (e.g. SET memory_limit low with a large VARCHAR GROUP BY), plus lists/structs in group keys. Correctness is checked on hidden shapes.

title: Partition count(DISTINCT) radix table on the group-key hash only
hypothesis: Measured this round on a temp table t holding q16's join output (1.18M rows, 27.8k groups): count(DISTINCT x) GROUP BY G takes 102-145 ms wall, SELECT DISTINCT G,x takes 65 ms, and GROUP BY G count(*) takes 30 ms. So after the distinct table is built, about 40 ms of wall goes to re-aggregating the 1.18M distinct tuples into the main table (E0002/E0004 timers: main-HT sink ~180 ms CPU plus main finalize ~30 ms CPU). The distinct radix table partitions on hash(G,x), so every distinct partition holds tuples of every group. Each of the 8 distinct-finalize tasks (AggregateDistinctGrouping, physical_hash_aggregate.cpp:648) therefore feeds all 28k groups into its local main HT. That HT has capacity 32768 and a resize threshold of 21845, so it abandons repeatedly, and the main finalize then combines about 8x or more duplicate group rows. If the radix bits of the distinct table's stored hash come from hash(G) alone, each distinct partition holds complete groups. Then each task's main local HT only sees ~28k*(partitions handled)/(total partitions) groups: it stays small and cache-resident, never abandons, and the main combine/finalize handles ~1x the groups. Salt (top 16 bits) and slot bits (low bits) keep coming from the full hash(G,x), so probe quality in the distinct HT is unchanged.
plan: 1) GroupedAggregateHashTable (src/execution/aggregate_hashtable.cpp + header): add an optional member `idx_t partition_key_count = 0` (0 = off) with a setter. Add a private helper `HashGroups(DataChunk &groups, Vector &hashes)`. It calls groups.Hash(hashes). When partition_key_count > 0 it also hashes only the first partition_key_count columns into a scratch HASH vector (DataChunk::Hash with a column subset, or VectorOperations::Hash/CombineHash over those columns in the same order DataChunk::Hash uses, so the values equal what the main table computes for G). It then splices: h = (h_full & ~RadixPartitioning::Mask(RadixPartitioning::MAX_RADIX_BITS)) | (h_G & Mask(MAX_RADIX_BITS)), i.e. bits [36,48) come from G. Use the helper at every place this HT hashes raw groups: AddChunk(groups,payload,filter) ~line 528, the dictionary/constant paths in TryAddCompressedGroups (~lines 428 and 480; simplest is to skip TryAddCompressedGroups when the option is on), and FindOrCreateGroups(groups, addresses, new_groups) ~line 830. Combine, Repartition and finalize reuse the stored hash column, so they stay consistent. 2) RadixPartitionedHashTable (src/execution/radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp): add a field set at construction and pass it to the HT in CreateHT (line 71). 3) DistinctAggregateData constructor (src/execution/operator/aggregate/distinct_aggregate_data.cpp:75-115): when group_expressions is non-null and groups is non-empty, set partition_key_count = groups.size() on the radix table. grouping_set is an ordered set with the group indices (< group_by_size) first, so the first groups.size() HT columns are exactly G in the same order as the main table's grouping set. Optional gate: skip when the aggregate's estimated_cardinality is small (e.g. < 4096 estimated groups), where few groups would skew the distinct partitions. Check q16's estimate with EXPLAIN before choosing the threshold, so q16 is not gated off. 4) Verify: results of q16 plus count(DISTINCT) with GROUPING SETS/ROLLUP, multiple distinct aggregates on different columns, distinct with FILTER, a NULL group key, and spilling (memory_limit 100MB). Bench q16. If the gain is small, check that the main local HT really stops abandoning, e.g. with a temporary counter.
expected_gain: q16: 5-12%. It removes most of the ~210 ms CPU in the main re-sink and finalize (about 15-25 ms wall of ~180).
generality: Any grouped DISTINCT aggregate (count/sum/avg DISTINCT ... GROUP BY) with many groups, such as TPC-H q16 and the 'distinct users per key' pattern. It could get slower when there are very few groups and many distinct values (e.g. GROUP BY a boolean): the distinct partitions become skewed and finalize parallelism drops. The estimated-cardinality gate limits that case. Ungrouped DISTINCT is untouched.
risk: Medium-low. Correctness only needs every insert into the distinct HT to use the same hash function. The risk is missing a hash site, e.g. the dictionary fast path or FindOrCreateGroups overloads, which would produce duplicate distinct tuples and wrong counts. Needs careful audit plus tests with dictionary-encoded group columns. The HLL in FindOrCreateGroupsInternal sees a slightly less random hash, which has negligible effect on adaptivity.

title: Evaluate small integral constant IN lists inline instead of a MARK join
hypothesis: In q16 the part scan emits 1,856,009 rows (0.10s CPU). The pushed `p_size IN (8 consts)` is only an OptionalFilter, used for zonemap pruning (filter_combiner.cpp:580-585). InClauseRewriter::VisitReplace (in_clause_rewriter.cpp:60) turns IN lists with >=6 constants into a MARK join against a COLUMN_DATA_SCAN, followed by a FILTER on the mark column. So every one of the 1.86M part rows is hashed, probed and marked before 84% of them are dropped. All of this happens in the join build pipeline, which has to finish before the partsupp probe pipeline starts, so it sits on the critical path. For a short list of integer constants, a vectorized membership test (a few compares per row, or a bitmap) is much cheaper than a hash-join probe. It also lets the FILTER put the cheap integer predicate ahead of the string predicates (brand <>, NOT LIKE).
plan: 1) src/optimizer/in_clause_rewriter.cpp InClauseRewriter::VisitReplace: before the mark-join path (after the `< 6` check), return nullptr (keep the BoundOperatorExpression COMPARE_IN/NOT_IN unchanged) when all of these hold: children[0]->return_type is an integral physical type of at most 64 bits (INT8..INT64, UINT8..UINT64; no HUGEINT, no DECIMAL needed), every child from 1 on is a non-NULL BoundConstantExpression, and children.size()-1 <= 64. 2) src/execution/expression_executor/execute_operator.cpp: add a fast path to the COMPARE_IN/NOT_IN branch (line 23) for the same condition. Cast the constants to int64 (or to the physical type), then evaluate the left vector with UnifiedVectorFormat. If max-min < 4096, test with a bitmap (vector<bool>/bitset built per call, or cached in ExpressionState if simple); otherwise use a sorted array with binary search. Write a BOOLEAN result that is NULL where the left side is NULL and true/false (inverted for NOT IN) otherwise. Keep the existing generic loop for everything else. Make sure the Select path (filter) goes through this Execute path or add a Select specialization. Check that the FILTER over part.p_size now evaluates IN directly and that the MARK join is gone from the q16 EXPLAIN.
expected_gain: q16 3-6% wall: removes a 1.86M-row mark-join probe and its hash from the serial build-side pipeline (scan+filter+mark ~0.13s+ CPU).
generality: Any query with a filter or projection of the form int_col [NOT] IN (6..64 integer constants), which is very common in TPC-H/DS-style workloads (sizes, years, ids). Lists with more than 64 values, non-integral types and non-constant lists keep the mark join. Possible slowdown: a 64-value list with a wide range uses binary search, which is still cheaper than a hash probe.
risk: Low-medium. NULL semantics: left NULL gives NULL. Constants are non-NULL by the gate, so NOT IN has no NULL-in-list edge case. Integer constants must already be cast to the left type (the binder does this); assert or bail out if the types differ.

title: Bypass main HT for all-distinct aggregates with group-aligned distinct partitions
hypothesis: After E0005 every distinct radix partition holds complete groups, but AggregateDistinctGrouping (physical_hash_aggregate.cpp:666-772) still re-sinks every distinct tuple (1.18M) into a local main HT, then runs Combine and HashAggregateFinalizeEvent. HASH_GROUP_BY is still 0.45-0.73s CPU, and in the R5 temp-table test re-aggregation cost ~40 ms wall of ~150.
plan: When partition_key_count is set and CanSkipRegularSink() holds, have each distinct-finalize task keep a local main HT per distinct partition sized to that partition. Skip the global combine by writing the finalized groups directly into a per-partition result collection that the main source scans.
generality: GROUP BY queries whose aggregates are all DISTINCT
risk: High: large change to the source and finalize state machine.
